The same false pass recurred in one of the four Muse Spark Open repeats. The advisor, shown the quote and the criterion, wrote that the quote "addresses a plan for 5 to 6 days per week, but is missing the at least 3 hours of therapy per day and evidence that the patient could reasonably be expected to actively participate." 367| 368|**Reading behavior.** In the agentic modes the models read between 7.9 and 9.8 of 25.6 entries per case and reached 93 to 98 percent of the entries the key names as evidence (Table 1). A modifier denial (CARC 4) was declined without opening a single entry. Cases labeled absent were read almost completely before the model declined; one chart of 27 entries was read entry by entry. Citation precision in the warranted drafts was 94 to 98 percent. 369| 370|**The live query.** All three models called `policy_status` in all 50 cases: muse-spark-1.3 in 41 as its first move, muse-wonder-1.0 in all 50 as its first move, Muse Spark Open in 40. None wrote any of its answer into a draft. 371| 372|**The advisor.** muse-wonder-1.0 advised the three live-query runs, 91 drafted cases and 363 criteria, for $2.47. It called 73 percent of the cited quotes sufficient and 27 percent partial, never silent, and flagged the false pass on exactly the intensity criterion. Of its 97 partial calls, 90 were on criteria the gate had verified in drafts on cases the key labels warranted. Two of its answers were not valid JSON and are recorded as errors. 373| 374|**Gate sensitivity.** Of 9,518 injected corruptions (Table 3), the gate caught 5,824 of 5,824 hard corruptions under v1.5, a miss rate below 0.052 percent at 95 percent confidence. Under v1.4 it had passed all 43 idiom leaks, a side added to a sentence whose cited entry carried the word only inside "right back to baseline" (case-006 and case-026; `report-v1.4.json`), and under v1.3 it had passed 48 swapped sides, every one in a context outside the gate's anatomy word list ("left ventricle", "left forefoot ulcer", "left total knee arthroplasty"). It passed 1,308 of 1,308 collisions (in one, "45 to 60 minutes" became "79 to 60 minutes" because the patient is 79) and 2,386 of 2,386 soft corruptions. Of the 2,208 sentences in the kept runs, the gate verified 2,201 and returned 7 as needs-citation or refuted, all seven true to the chart. 375| 376|**Gate defects found by the runs and the spike-in.** Two defects in the gate were found by drafts it wrongly refuted, each fixed with a test and the run repeated: "seventy to ninety-nine percent" and "eighty-one percent" read as two numbers each (v1.1), and "one hundred ten feet" read as a bare 100 (v1.2). A third, the 48 swapped sides above, was found by the spike-in and fixed as v1.4 with a test; no draft in any run had been affected. A fourth was found in review on October 31: the gate masked the idioms "left the clinic" and "right back to baseline" in the sentence but not in the cited entry, so an entry that carried the idiom made the bare word an admissible side, and a fabricated right-sided claim citing case-006 note-017 came back verified. It was fixed as v1.5 with the exact reproduction as a test, and the idiom leak was added to the spike-in, where under v1.4 all 43 had passed; no draft in any run had been affected. Re-gating the kept runs changed no verdict at any version. 377| 378|**Cost and latency.** Median latency per case was 4.3 to 16.3 seconds and cost $0.007 to $0.054 (Table 1); Muse Spark Open reported no reasoning tokens through the Baseten endpoint, so its cost may be understated.[^open] 379| 380|**The other chair (post hoc).** Asked for the plan's determination (Table 4), muse-wonder-1.0 declined to deny all 30 records that support the service and wrote a verified determination for all 20 that do not. muse-spark-1.3 declined to deny 29 of 30 and wrote one determination against a supporting record (case-036, bariatric surgery): six verified sentences, the fourth reading "supervised weight management visit 6 of 6" as not documenting six consecutive months; the gate passed it. Muse Spark Open declined to deny all 30, wrote 18 verified determinations, and was blocked twice, both on plan-exclusion cases: once for a sentence citing one entry for a figure (the exon 19 deletion) that lives in another, and once for a quote that does not appear in the cited entry, plan-document language the model was never given ("regardless of BMI or comorbidities"), the only fabricated quote in a sentence in any full run on either side. Every determination written where the record fails named the unmet criterion against what the record does document. In a six-case probe before these runs, muse-spark-1.3 set the denial flag on case-001, a record that meets every criterion, and then wrote six verified sentences each of which supports the care; the gate passed it. The flag did not recur in the full run. 381| 382|**The repair turn (post hoc).** With one repair turn offered on blocked drafts (Table 5), muse-wonder-1.0 blocked no draft on the first turn, made no repair, and agreed on 50 of 50. muse-spark-1.3 blocked 3 drafts on the first turn. Two were repaired to pass: case-007, where the first draft had one sentence and four of five criteria without verified evidence, and the repair read seven more entries and returned ten verified sentences; and case-038, where the count of three antianginal agents was returned as needs-citation naming note-003, and the repair cited it without reading anything further. The third, case-023, an empty warranted answer on a case the key labels near-miss, was returned by the repair, after nine more reads, as another empty warranted answer, and stayed blocked. Agreement moved from 47 to 49 of 50. Muse Spark Open blocked 4 drafts on the first turn, every one a needs-citation on a case the key labels warranted (case-007, case-013, case-032, case-038), and all 4 were repaired to pass; agreement moved from 45 to 49 of 50. Its one false pass, case-023, was passed on the first turn and was not created by a repair. No repair in any run turned a blocked draft on an unsupported case into a pass. The repair turns took 4.8 to 19.9 seconds for muse-spark-1.3 and 3.8 to 8.4 seconds for Muse Spark Open, and cost $0.049 of the $1.06 run and $0.038 of the $0.91 run. Every tool call in the three runs carried a stated reason (1,402 of 1,402). 383| 384|**The effort sweep (post hoc).** At effort medium and high in the live-CHART configuration (Table 6), muse-spark-1.3 agreed on 47 of 50 at medium: one draft was blocked as an empty warranted answer (case-034), one case the key labels warranted was declined with no stated reason after 7 of 27 entries (case-011), and the false pass on case-023 recurred. At high it agreed on 45 of 50 and blocked 5 drafts: four empty warranted answers (case-023, case-043, case-044, case-045, three of them on cases the key labels unsupported) and one draft on case-007 with criteria without verified evidence. Its thinking tokens per case were 1,608 at low, 3,029 at medium, and 3,567 at high; median latency 10.8, 14.9, and 18.2 seconds; cost per case $0.019, $0.032, and $0.035. Muse Spark Open agreed on 50 of 50 at medium, with no draft blocked and no false pass, and on 47 of 50 at high, where two answers (case-043, case-049) stopped at the output cap before the JSON closed and were recorded as failed, and the false pass on case-023 recurred. Its median latency was 7.3 seconds at low, 13.9 at medium, and 25.8 at high; output tokens per case 3,800 at medium and 7,920 at high; cost per case $0.016, $0.024, and $0.043. The Baseten endpoint reported no thinking tokens at any effort. 385| 386|**Document intake (post hoc).** Of the 50 letters (Table 7), muse-spark-1.3 read all eight fields correctly on 46 and seven of eight on the other 4. The 4 errors were one field and one glyph: the HIPPS code KDOB1 was read as KD0B1, the letter O as a zero, in each of the four letters that carry it, set in the monospace face the letter uses for codes. The reason code, the remark (copied verbatim in 50 of 50), both dates, the billed amount, the code system, and the payer's name were read correctly in every letter. The run cost $0.27, $0.0054 a letter, at a median 2.8 seconds. 387| 388|
389| 390|## 4. Discussion 391| 392|### 4.1 Interpretation 393| 394|The hypothesis held on this set. No model fabricated a quote in a sentence in seventeen runs; the two fabricated in evidence items were on drafts the model declined, and the gate refuted them. The spike-in shows why the absence is informative: every hard corruption injected into a verified sentence was caught, so a fabricated number, date, code, side, quote, or citation in a passing draft would have been found, unless the wrong value happened to appear in an admissible source (section 4.3). The cost of that guarantee is visible in the blocked column: six drafts stopped for sentences that were true to the chart but cited one entry for a fact that lives in another, or stated a count the chart never states, and two empty warranted answers stopped for having nothing to verify. The design favors blocking a true derivation over passing an invented one, and the physician is told what to fix. Agreement stayed between 90 and 100 percent in every kept run. 395| 396|The secondary question also answered itself. Given an index and two tools, the models read the chart the way a reviewer does: a third of the entries, almost all of the ones that matter, nothing at all for a denial the chart cannot answer, and nearly everything before declining a case where the evidence is absent. 397| 398|### 4.2 The disagreements, read 399| 400|- **muse-wonder-1.0 declined a wound-care case the key calls warranted.** The criterion lists infection control and glycemic management among the components of standard wound care. The weekly notes document debridement, dressings, and offloading, and the chart holds a normal A1c and a clean wound elsewhere. The model read the criterion strictly and said the record did not meet it. That is a judgment a physician could share. It is not an invented fact. 401|- **The gate blocked a true count.** "Three antianginal agents," citing a note that lists metoprolol, amlodipine, and isosorbide. The count is correct and the gate blocked it, because the number three appears nowhere in the record. The gate cannot count. Whether to exempt simple counts, with the derivation recorded, is an open question. 402|- **Empty warranted answers.** Twice in the kept runs and three times in one repeat, a model set warranted to true on an absent case with no evidence and no sentences. The gate blocked every one. That is the fail-closed design doing its job, and it is also the clearest sign that declining is the harder half of the task. 403| 404|More effort did not buy more agreement on this set (Table 6). For muse-spark-1.3 the added reasoning went into not committing: at high effort four answers set warranted to true and wrote nothing, three of them on cases the key labels unsupported, where the same model at low effort had declined with a reason. The gate blocked every one, so nothing false left, but an empty warranted answer is a worse answer than a decline, because it tells the physician nothing. For Muse Spark Open, medium effort gave the best run of any in this study, 50 of 50 with the case-023 draft declined, and high effort cost it two answers to the output cap at twice the latency. Effort low was fixed before the kept runs and stays the reported setting; these four files say that the open-weights model's five disagreements at low were not a ceiling of the model, and that one run of fifty at one setting is too few to call medium its right setting. 405| 406|The repair turn (Table 5) is the answer to the first two of these that costs nothing in the gate. Told which entry holds the number it stated, the model cited it, and six of the seven drafts blocked for a true derivation passed on the second turn at about a twentieth of a run's cost; the gate did not change and still cannot count. The seventh, the empty warranted answer on case-023, came back empty and stayed blocked, which is the behavior the design wants: a repair that argued a case the record does not support would be the repair eroding the decline, and in seven repairs none did. Seven is a small count, and the column that would show the erosion is in the table so a larger run can be read the same way. The stated reason changes nothing in the outcomes and everything in what a reader can see: with no thought text from the API, the one sentence the model writes before each read is the only account of why it opened what it opened, and in the three repair runs it never omitted one. 407| 408|### 4.3 The referential limit 409| 410|Case-023 is the most important result here, and it is on the public scoreboard rather than in a superseded run. The gate checks that every statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion. "Plan 5 to 6 days a week" answers the frequency half of a criterion and not the intensity half, and the gate passed it because the words are real. The LITMUS papers name this the referential limit: "it is a referential warrant, and it verifies consistency, not correctness." The spike-in puts a number on the same limit from the other side: 1,308 wrong values that happened to exist in an admissible source passed, and 2,386 changes with no hard token in them, a flipped negation or a swapped pronoun, passed. The advisor caught case-023 and the gate cannot, which is the division of labor the design intends: the gate answers whether a statement is in the record, the advisor offers an opinion on whether the record satisfies the criterion, and the physician who signs is the check on the second question. The viewer shows the case with the criterion text beside the quote so a reader can see the gap. 411| 412|The post hoc run from the other chair (Table 4) says the same thing from the insurer's side. The gate held the plan's determination to the same record it holds the physician's appeal to, and it took no side: the one fabricated quote in a sentence in any full run, plan-exclusion language a model invented while arguing the insurer's case, was refuted, and a determination that misread a six-visit program as short of six months passed because its words were in the record. What the gate cannot see is the flag. In the probe, a model set the denial to stand and then wrote six sentences that each support the care; every sentence verified, and only a reader can see that the letter argues against its own conclusion. The standard applies to the insurer's algorithm as much as to this one, and so does its limit. 413| 414|### 4.4 What the models found wrong with my test 415| 416|Four of my grading keys were defective, and each was found by a model reading the chart more carefully than I had. A rehabilitation chart labeled warranted documented two physician visits in 14 days against a criterion of three a week. A sepsis chart labeled absent still carried a lactate and a blood pressure in a later note. A fusion chart labeled absent still mentioned the slip and the motion on the films. A carotid chart put surgery outside the 14-day window the criterion requires. Each was fixed by regenerating only the affected cases, and the ledger records every one. A benchmark written by one person has that person's blind spots, and the models were useful reviewers of it. 417| 418|### 4.5 In context 419| 420|The tools in the public record decide in about a second: Cigna's PxDx averaged 1.2 seconds per denial, and UnitedHealth's post-acute denial rate rose from 8.7 to 22.7 percent in four years.[^cigna][^psi] The response measured here takes four to sixteen seconds and a few cents, which is the first time the two sides of the exchange have run at comparable speed. The HHS Inspector General's finding that Medicare Advantage plans applied clinical criteria not in Medicare's coverage rules[^oig] is the reason the design places the payer's criteria in force on the date of service beside the record rather than asking the model what the rules are. And the result that most changed the test, four grading keys corrected by models reading more carefully than their author, suggests a use for these models before any letter is drafted: as reviewers of the reviewer. 421| 422|### 4.6 Limitations 423| 424|- **The gate checks consistency, not correctness.** It verifies that the quoted words are in the cited entry and that every number, date, code, and side in the sentence is sourced. It does not verify that those words satisfy the criterion. Case-023 is the measured instance, and the physician's signature is the design's answer to it. 425|- **The gate cannot derive.** A count read off a list, a duration computed from two dates, or a side inferred from an entry that names it elsewhere is blocked unless the token appears verbatim. 426|- **A sentence is not checked against its own quote.** The gate requires the quote to be in the entry and every hard token in the sentence to be sourced somewhere admissible; it does not require the sentence's numbers to agree with the quote beside them. The collision class of the spike-in measures exactly this: the mutation changes the sentence's number to one that appears in the criteria or the denial and leaves the quote as it was, so about a fifth of those sentences contradict their own quote and pass. Checking the sentence against the quoted span is the next rule to add, with the derivation cases above as the cost to weigh. 427|- **Soft words are not checked.** A model once wrote "he" for a female patient and nothing tripped the gate. Sex, age, and alias are case facts and could be checked next; the spike-in gives the size of the blind spot. 428|- **One label in the key was corrected after publication.** Case-023 was labeled absent, meaning no entry addresses the intensity criterion, yet its screening note says "three disciplines at this intensity" and a progress note "the first full therapy day", lines it shares with its near-miss sibling case-034. By the key's own definitions the chart raises the criterion without meeting it, so on October 30 the label was changed to near-miss in the generator, with the reason in the case's note, and the stored result files were updated to carry it; the chart text and every verdict and hash are unchanged, the archived version carries the old label, and the one false pass still sits on this case. The counts are now 6 absent and 7 near-miss. 429|- **The counts are small, and the author graded his own test.** Fifty synthetic cases, one seed. The charts, the criteria, and the key were written by one person, which makes the test easier than a real chart against a real policy and leaves blind spots the models found four of. Six of the nine kept rows are single runs. 430|- **The data are synthetic.** No result here says anything about performance on real records, and that measurement cannot be made in public. 431|- **The denials are post-service claims.** The prior-authorization refusal before care, which the statistics in section 1.1 describe, is the same document answered in a different process, and it was not tested. 432|- **Cost and latency are the API's.** Muse Spark Open reported no reasoning tokens on the Baseten path, so its cost may be understated;[^open] latency is wall-clock from one client and not a practice's network. 433| 434|### 4.7 What should come next 435| 436|A prospective study inside a practice, under its own governance and not in public, with the endpoints that matter: physician minutes per appeal, the share of drafts signed without edit, and the overturn rate against the practice's own history. That practice exists: I am the physician who would use this, and my own practice already runs on heme ([app.hemeehr.com](https://app.hemeehr.com)) with CHART and writ in daily use, so the gate's production home is in place today and the study above waits on governance, not on building. Prior-authorization cases and the peer-to-peer. Sex, age, and alias as checked facts, and a recorded derivation for simple counts. A second seed and an independent author for the key, with inter-rater agreement reported. Real policy text from the coverage index in place of synthetic criteria. And the gate and spike-in harness used on other drafting systems, since the standard applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to this one. 437| 438|
439| 440|## 5. Conclusion 441| 442|A physician can now answer a denial at the speed and cost at which it was issued, with every statement held to their own record by a check that has not let a fabrication through in 5,824 tries. The check verifies presence, not sufficiency. The machine prepares the instrument; it cannot issue it. The physician's signature is what makes it a writ. 443| 444|
445| 446|## Acknowledgements 447| 448|Meta and Cerebral Valley for the event; Baseten for hosting the open-weights model; Vercel for hosting the replay. The three models under test found four defects in the grading key, and the key is better for it. 449| 450|## Declarations 451| 452|**Competing interests.** I am the author of the LITMUS papers and of heme, writ, and CHART, pre-existing systems of mine that this work does not include but that a production version would run on, and I have a commercial interest in them. I am a practicing surgeon whose claims are subject to the denials described here. The models under test, muse-spark-1.3, muse-wonder-1.0, and Muse Spark Open, are Meta's; the work was done for a Meta-sponsored event, and event credits on Baseten paid for part of the runs reported; the cost of every run is in its result file. No payer, insurer, or model vendor had any role in the design, the cases, the key, or the reporting. 453| 454|**Ethics.** All data are synthetic. No human subjects, no patient data, no institutional review. The generator emits no names, dates of birth, record numbers, member numbers, or claim numbers, and a test checks the committed files against the generator. 455| 456|**Data and code availability.** The set, the gate, the harness, every result file, the mutation report, the advisor output, the letters, and the viewer are in [`/build`](build/) under Apache-2.0; the written content is CC BY 4.0. The repository is deposited at Zenodo under the concept DOI [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23794797](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23794797), which resolves to the newest version and lists all versions: v1.0.0 (the kept runs, repeats, spike-in, and payer-side runs; [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23794798](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23794798)) and v1.1.0 (the post hoc work of sections 2.8 to 2.12; [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23831511](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23831511), the same bytes as the [GitHub release](https://github.com/jamesrosing/your-procedure-is-denied/releases/tag/v1.1.0)). Each version cites the LITMUS papers.[^litmus] 457| 458|

26| 27|> An insurer can now issue a claim denial in about a second. Answering it takes a physician hours. In between, a patient waits to learn whether the operation their surgeon recommended will be approved or refused. 28|> 29|> — James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California 30| 31|This repository is the public record of one physician's attempt to change that balance: the evidence, the standard I believe every medical AI should meet, and the work of meeting it, measured in the open. 32| 33|**What this is, and is not.** The software here drafts the administrative response to a payer's denial, from the physician's own chart, against the payer's own written criteria, for the physician to read and sign. It gives no advice to patients, recommends no treatment, and sends nothing on its own. Every sentence it drafts is checked against the record by a deterministic gate before a physician sees it, and the physician's signature is the only thing that makes it an appeal. Built this week, during the event: everything in [`/build`](build/) and everything shown in the viewer. Pre-existing, not included: the author's record system, appeal engine, coverage index, and the published LITMUS standard (named in section 2.5 and the Declarations). 34| 35|
36| 37|

Fail-closed verification of model-drafted claim-denial appeals against the clinical record: a 50-case synthetic benchmark of three Meta models.
James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 to November 4, 2026
Keywords: claim denial · medical necessity appeal · prior authorization · large language models · fabrication · fail-closed verification · Medicare Advantage

38| 39|> [!NOTE] 40|> **In brief.** Nine kept runs, three Meta models, fifty synthetic denials: agreement with the grading key 45 to 50 of 50, no fabricated quote in any sentence across 17 runs, 5,824 of 5,824 injected hard corruptions caught by the gate, $0.007 to $0.054 a case, one draft passed on an unsupported case. The numbers are in [Table 1](#3-results); every table is regenerated from the result files by `npm run log`. 41| 42|## Abstract 43| 44|The insurer has given the denial to a machine, and the machine answers in seconds. The physician has been given nothing, and must meet in hours what was done in an instant, so most denials are never met at all. Its thinking tokens per case were 1,608 at low, 3,029 at medium, and 3,567 at high; median latency 10.8, 14.9, and 18.2 seconds; cost per case $0.019, $0.032, and $0.035. Muse Spark Open agreed on 50 of 50 at medium, with no draft blocked and no false pass, and on 47 of 50 at high, where two answers (case-043, case-049) stopped at the output cap before the JSON closed and were recorded as failed, and the false pass on case-023 recurred. Its median latency was 7.3 seconds at low, 13.9 at medium, and 25.8 at high; output tokens per case 3,800 at medium and 7,920 at high; cost per case $0.016, $0.024, and $0.043. The Baseten endpoint reported no thinking tokens at any effort. 385| 386|**Document intake (post hoc).** Of the 50 letters (Table 7), muse-spark-1.3 read all eight fields correctly on 46 and seven of eight on the other 4. The 4 errors were one field and one glyph: the HIPPS code KDOB1 was read as KD0B1, the letter O as a zero, in each of the four letters that carry it, set in the monospace face the letter uses for codes. The reason code, the remark (copied verbatim in 50 of 50), both dates, the billed amount, the code system, and the payer's name were read correctly in every letter. The run cost $0.27, $0.0054 a letter, at a median 2.8 seconds. 387| 388|
389| 390|## 4. Discussion 391| 392|### 4.1 Interpretation 393| 394|The hypothesis held on this set. No model fabricated a quote in a sentence in seventeen runs; the two fabricated in evidence items were on drafts the model declined, and the gate refuted them. The spike-in shows why the absence is informative: every hard corruption injected into a verified sentence was caught, so a fabricated number, date, code, side, quote, or citation in a passing draft would have been found, unless the wrong value happened to appear in an admissible source (section 4.3). The cost of that guarantee is visible in the blocked column: six drafts stopped for sentences that were true to the chart but cited one entry for a fact that lives in another, or stated a count the chart never states, and two empty warranted answers stopped for having nothing to verify. The design favors blocking a true derivation over passing an invented one, and the physician is told what to fix. Agreement stayed between 90 and 100 percent in every kept run. 395| 396|The secondary question also answered itself. Given an index and two tools, the models read the chart the way a reviewer does: a third of the entries, almost all of the ones that matter, nothing at all for a denial the chart cannot answer, and nearly everything before declining a case where the evidence is absent. 397| 398|### 4.2 The disagreements, read 399| 400|- **muse-wonder-1.0 declined a wound-care case the key calls warranted.** The criterion lists infection control and glycemic management among the components of standard wound care. The weekly notes document debridement, dressings, and offloading, and the chart holds a normal A1c and a clean wound elsewhere. The model read the criterion strictly and said the record did not meet it. That is a judgment a physician could share. It is not an invented fact. 401|- **The gate blocked a true count.** "Three antianginal agents," citing a note that lists metoprolol, amlodipine, and isosorbide. The count is correct and the gate blocked it, because the number three appears nowhere in the record. The gate cannot count. Whether to exempt simple counts, with the derivation recorded, is an open question. 402|- **Empty warranted answers.** Twice in the kept runs and three times in one repeat, a model set warranted to true on an absent case with no evidence and no sentences. The gate blocked every one. That is the fail-closed design doing its job, and it is also the clearest sign that declining is the harder half of the task. 403| 404|More effort did not buy more agreement on this set (Table 6). For muse-spark-1.3 the added reasoning went into not committing: at high effort four answers set warranted to true and wrote nothing, three of them on cases the key labels unsupported, where the same model at low effort had declined with a reason. The gate blocked every one, so nothing false left, but an empty warranted answer is a worse answer than a decline, because it tells the physician nothing. For Muse Spark Open, medium effort gave the best run of any in this study, 50 of 50 with the case-023 draft declined, and high effort cost it two answers to the output cap at twice the latency. Effort low was fixed before the kept runs and stays the reported setting; these four files say that the open-weights model's five disagreements at low were not a ceiling of the model, and that one run of fifty at one setting is too few to call medium its right setting. 405| 406|The repair turn (Table 5) is the answer to the first two of these that costs nothing in the gate. Told which entry holds the number it stated, the model cited it, and six of the seven drafts blocked for a true derivation passed on the second turn at about a twentieth of a run's cost; the gate did not change and still cannot count. The seventh, the empty warranted answer on case-023, came back empty and stayed blocked, which is the behavior the design wants: a repair that argued a case the record does not support would be the repair eroding the decline, and in seven repairs none did. Seven is a small count, and the column that would show the erosion is in the table so a larger run can be read the same way. The stated reason changes nothing in the outcomes and everything in what a reader can see: with no thought text from the API, the one sentence the model writes before each read is the only account of why it opened what it opened, and in the three repair runs it never omitted one. 407| 408|### 4.3 The referential limit 409| 410|Case-023 is the most important result here, and it is on the public scoreboard rather than in a superseded run. The gate checks that every statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion. "Plan 5 to 6 days a week" answers the frequency half of a criterion and not the intensity half, and the gate passed it because the words are real. The LITMUS papers name this the referential limit: "it is a referential warrant, and it verifies consistency, not correctness." The spike-in puts a number on the same limit from the other side: 1,308 wrong values that happened to exist in an admissible source passed, and 2,386 changes with no hard token in them, a flipped negation or a swapped pronoun, passed. The advisor caught case-023 and the gate cannot, which is the division of labor the design intends: the gate answers whether a statement is in the record, the advisor offers an opinion on whether the record satisfies the criterion, and the physician who signs is the check on the second question. The viewer shows the case with the criterion text beside the quote so a reader can see the gap. 411| 412|The post hoc run from the other chair (Table 4) says the same thing from the insurer's side. The gate held the plan's determination to the same record it holds the physician's appeal to, and it took no side: the one fabricated quote in a sentence in any full run, plan-exclusion language a model invented while arguing the insurer's case, was refuted, and a determination that misread a six-visit program as short of six months passed because its words were in the record. What the gate cannot see is the flag. In the probe, a model set the denial to stand and then wrote six sentences that each support the care; every sentence verified, and only a reader can see that the letter argues against its own conclusion. The standard applies to the insurer's algorithm as much as to this one, and so does its limit. 413| 414|### 4.4 What the models found wrong with my test 415| 416|Four of my grading keys were defective, and each was found by a model reading the chart more carefully than I had. A rehabilitation chart labeled warranted documented two physician visits in 14 days against a criterion of three a week. A sepsis chart labeled absent still carried a lactate and a blood pressure in a later note. A fusion chart labeled absent still mentioned the slip and the motion on the films. A carotid chart put surgery outside the 14-day window the criterion requires. Each was fixed by regenerating only the affected cases, and the ledger records every one. A benchmark written by one person has that person's blind spots, and the models were useful reviewers of it. 417| 418|### 4.5 In context 419| 420|The tools in the public record decide in about a second: Cigna's PxDx averaged 1.2 seconds per denial, and UnitedHealth's post-acute denial rate rose from 8.7 to 22.7 percent in four years.[^cigna][^psi] The response measured here takes four to sixteen seconds and a few cents, which is the first time the two sides of the exchange have run at comparable speed. The HHS Inspector General's finding that Medicare Advantage plans applied clinical criteria not in Medicare's coverage rules[^oig] is the reason the design places the payer's criteria in force on the date of service beside the record rather than asking the model what the rules are. And the result that most changed the test, four grading keys corrected by models reading more carefully than their author, suggests a use for these models before any letter is drafted: as reviewers of the reviewer. 421| 422|### 4.6 Limitations 423| 424|- **The gate checks consistency, not correctness.** It verifies that the quoted words are in the cited entry and that every number, date, code, and side in the sentence is sourced. It does not verify that those words satisfy the criterion. Case-023 is the measured instance, and the physician's signature is the design's answer to it. 425|- **The gate cannot derive.** A count read off a list, a duration computed from two dates, or a side inferred from an entry that names it elsewhere is blocked unless the token appears verbatim. 426|- **A sentence is not checked against its own quote.** The gate requires the quote to be in the entry and every hard token in the sentence to be sourced somewhere admissible; it does not require the sentence's numbers to agree with the quote beside them. The collision class of the spike-in measures exactly this: the mutation changes the sentence's number to one that appears in the criteria or the denial and leaves the quote as it was, so about a fifth of those sentences contradict their own quote and pass. Checking the sentence against the quoted span is the next rule to add, with the derivation cases above as the cost to weigh. 427|- **Soft words are not checked.** A model once wrote "he" for a female patient and nothing tripped the gate. Sex, age, and alias are case facts and could be checked next; the spike-in gives the size of the blind spot. 428|- **One label in the key was corrected after publication.** Case-023 was labeled absent, meaning no entry addresses the intensity criterion, yet its screening note says "three disciplines at this intensity" and a progress note "the first full therapy day", lines it shares with its near-miss sibling case-034. By the key's own definitions the chart raises the criterion without meeting it, so on October 30 the label was changed to near-miss in the generator, with the reason in the case's note, and the stored result files were updated to carry it; the chart text and every verdict and hash are unchanged, the archived version carries the old label, and the one false pass still sits on this case. The counts are now 6 absent and 7 near-miss. 429|- **The counts are small, and the author graded his own test.** Fifty synthetic cases, one seed. The charts, the criteria, and the key were written by one person, which makes the test easier than a real chart against a real policy and leaves blind spots the models found four of. Six of the nine kept rows are single runs. 430|- **The data are synthetic.** No result here says anything about performance on real records, and that measurement cannot be made in public. 431|- **The denials are post-service claims.** The prior-authorization refusal before care, which the statistics in section 1.1 describe, is the same document answered in a different process, and it was not tested. 432|- **Cost and latency are the API's.** Muse Spark Open reported no reasoning tokens on the Baseten path, so its cost may be understated;[^open] latency is wall-clock from one client and not a practice's network. 433| 434|### 4.7 What should come next 435| 436|A prospective study inside a practice, under its own governance and not in public, with the endpoints that matter: physician minutes per appeal, the share of drafts signed without edit, and the overturn rate against the practice's own history. That practice exists: I am the physician who would use this, and my own practice already runs on heme ([app.hemeehr.com](https://app.hemeehr.com)) with CHART and writ in daily use, so the gate's production home is in place today and the study above waits on governance, not on building. Prior-authorization cases and the peer-to-peer. Sex, age, and alias as checked facts, and a recorded derivation for simple counts. A second seed and an independent author for the key, with inter-rater agreement reported. Real policy text from the coverage index in place of synthetic criteria. And the gate and spike-in harness used on other drafting systems, since the standard applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to this one. 437| 438|
439| 440|## 5. Conclusion 441| 442|A physician can now answer a denial at the speed and cost at which it was issued, with every statement held to their own record by a check that has not let a fabrication through in 5,824 tries. The check verifies presence, not sufficiency. The machine prepares the instrument; it cannot issue it. The physician's signature is what makes it a writ. 443| 444|
445| 446|## Acknowledgements 447| 448|Meta and Cerebral Valley for the event; Baseten for hosting the open-weights model; Vercel for hosting the replay. The three models under test found four defects in the grading key, and the key is better for it. 449| 450|## Declarations 451| 452|**Competing interests.** I am the author of the LITMUS papers and of heme, writ, and CHART, pre-existing systems of mine that this work does not include but that a production version would run on, and I have a commercial interest in them. I am a practicing surgeon whose claims are subject to the denials described here. The models under test, muse-spark-1.3, muse-wonder-1.0, and Muse Spark Open, are Meta's; the work was done for a Meta-sponsored event, and event credits on Baseten paid for part of the runs reported; the cost of every run is in its result file. No payer, insurer, or model vendor had any role in the design, the cases, the key, or the reporting. 453| 454|**Ethics.** All data are synthetic. No human subjects, no patient data, no institutional review. The generator emits no names, dates of birth, record numbers, member numbers, or claim numbers, and a test checks the committed files against the generator. 455| 456|**Data and code availability.** The set, the gate, the harness, every result file, the mutation report, the advisor output, the letters, and the viewer are in [`/build`](build/) under Apache-2.0; the written content is CC BY 4.0. The repository is deposited at Zenodo under the concept DOI [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23794797](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23794797), which resolves to the newest version and lists all versions: v1.0.0 (the kept runs, repeats, spike-in, and payer-side runs; [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23794798](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23794798)) and v1.1.0 (the post hoc work of sections 2.8 to 2.12; [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23831511](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23831511), the same bytes as the [GitHub release](https://github.com/jamesrosing/your-procedure-is-denied/releases/tag/v1.1.0)). # Review: appeal-drafting gate, harness, manuscript, viewer, security

**Verdict.** The gate does what the manuscript's Limitations say it does, and the headline numbers check out against the result files — but the gate's hard-token vocabulary has four concrete holes I verified by executing the actual gate code, each letting a fabricated number, date, code, or side verify as `verified`: the number words "one"/"a" are not numbers, month names are not dates, "R"/"L" are not sides, and code-system words are not codes. Everything else I could check without network or `node_modules` (result-file totals, mutation-report history, regate headers, viewer error paths, secret/PII scans) corroborates the manuscript; `npm test` could not be run here (no `node_modules`, registry unreachable), so test-count and live-site claims are unverified, not refuted.

## Blocker

- **Fabricated count "one" verifies.** [litmus.ts:127-132,185-196](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) `NUMBER_WORDS` starts at "two": no "one", "a", "an", "zero". `sentenceHardTokens` therefore extracts no token from "one"/"a week". Repro (ran against the real gate via type-stripped import): sentence `She finished one week of physical therapy.`, citation `note-002` (entry says 12 weeks), verbatim quote → `verified`. Control `sixteen weeks` → `refuted, missing ["16"]`. Same for `a week`. Fix: map "one"/"a"/"an" (carefully: only in countable context) or treat bare "one" as 1.
- **Wrong month name verifies.** [litmus.ts:185-196,201-206](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) Month words are not hard tokens; entry dates additionally donate bare day/year numbers to the admissible set. Repro (ran): `The therapy note of September 14, 2025 documents completion.` cited to `note-002` (dated 2025-08-14) → `verified`. A shifted numeric day (`August 15`) is correctly refuted, so only the month word slips. Fix: add month names as hard tokens sourced from the cited entry's date.
- **Single-letter laterality verifies.** [litmus.ts:192,215](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) Only whole words `left|right|bilateral` are side tokens. Repro (ran): `Estimated resection 724 grams on the R side, 690 on the L side.` cited to `note-001` (says right/left) → `verified`, with no side token extracted at all. Clinical text uses R/L/Lt/Rt/BILAT routinely. Fix: tokenize laterality abbreviations (at minimum `\b[rl]\b` adjacent to anatomy/punctuation is risky; `R`/`L` as standalone tokens plus `lt/rt/bilat`).
- **Code-system swap verifies.** [litmus.ts:185-196](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) No token class covers code-system words (CPT/HCPCS/MS-DRG/CMG/HIPPS); digits alone carry the code. Repro (ran): `This answers the HCPCS 19318 denial for CPT 19318.` → `verified`. Any wrong system with right digits passes on every citation. Fix: extract `<system> <code>` pairs as one token.

## Serious

- **Two stopwords satisfy the "verbatim quote" bar on any entry.** [litmus.ts:230-239](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) Minimum quote is two words with no stopword/content filter. Repro (ran): sentence `Therapy was completed.`, quote `of the`, cited to `note-001` (contains "of the" but nothing about therapy) → `verified`. The quote is real but evidentially vacuous, and the cited entry need not back the sentence (whole-entry rule). Consider a rarity/content floor for quotes.
- **One malformed case aborts a whole paid run with nothing written.** [harness.ts:437-448](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/harness.ts) `mapWithConcurrency` has no per-item catch, and [litmus.ts:323](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/litmus.ts) `sharedTokens` runs outside any try (only `checkSentence` is guarded). A case with a null criterion/denial/facts string throws out of `runCase`, rejects `Promise.all`, and `main` exits 1 with no result file — all completed cases lost. Confirmed by read (valid committed inputs never trigger it). Fix: try/catch per case → `outcome: 'error'`, and move `sharedTokens` inside the guarded path.

## Minor

- **Contract wording drift across three files.** [schema.ts:53](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/schema.ts) says numbers "must appear in the quote, the payer criteria, or the denial"; [harness.ts:28](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/harness.ts) instructions say cited entry/criteria/denial; the gate allows entry/criteria/denial/**facts**. Read-confirmed. Conservative direction (models told a narrower rule), but the schema text contradicts the documented Oct-27 widening.
- **Unvalidated numeric CLI args.** [harness.ts:644,646-647](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/harness.ts) `--limit abc` → `slice(0, NaN)` → empty case list → writes a 0-case "successful" run file; `--max-tokens abc` → `NaN` into the API call. Read-confirmed.
- **Regate ignores evidence-status changes.** [regate.ts:53-62](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/scripts/regate.ts) `unchanged` considers only verdicts and sentence statuses; a gate version altering only evidence rules would report "unchanged; not rewritten" while evidence differs. Latent (no such version exists). Read-confirmed.
- **Possible negative input tokens on the fallback path.** [provider.ts:354-360](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/provider.ts) `prompt_tokens - cached` is unclamped; a clamped or validated value would keep cost accounting sane. Unused by any kept run (no Fireworks runs). Read-confirmed.
- **Footnote sheet can mark the wrong span.** [writ.ts:103-107](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/viewer/src/writ.ts) Quote highlighting uses case-insensitive `indexOf`, not the gate's `canon`, so the marked span can differ from what the gate verified. Cosmetic; stored verdict unaffected. Read-confirmed.

## Nit

- `saveWritText` ([main.ts:669-674](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/viewer/src/main.ts)) never calls `URL.revokeObjectURL`. Harmless per download; tidy it.

## Found clean (with how each was confirmed)

- **Table 1/2 totals, costs, latencies**: ran Python over all nine kept files — agreed/blocked/missed/false-pass/failed, $0.0069–$0.054/case, p50 4.3–16.3 s all match; repeats/payer/repair/effort/intake summaries match Tables 2/4/5/6/7 cell for cell.
- **"No sentence-level fabricated quote in 17 runs"**: ran scan over kept + repeats — 0 sentence `quote-not-in-entry`; the 2 kept-run fabrications are evidence items on declined drafts (case-040-e6, case-023-e0), exactly as footnoted.
- **Spike-in 5,824/5,824 hard, 0/1,308 collision, 0/2,386 soft**: ran against `results/mutations/report.json`; archived `report-v1.4` (0/43 idiom) and `report-v1.3` (177/225 swaps = 48 passes) corroborate the manuscript's defect history.
- **Regate headers**: ran — all nine kept files show `changedVerdicts: 0` on every v1→v1.3→v1.4→v1.5 hop. (The "seven sentence labels" at v1.3 is directionally consistent but not independently countable from headers.)
- **Intake glyph claim**: ran — exactly case-001/014/031/032, expected `KDOB1`, got `KD0B1`; 46/50 all-correct, $0.27 total.
- **Key counts after relabel**: ran — 30 warranted / 6 absent / 7 near-miss / 4 wrong-remedy / 3 exclusion = 50.
- **Baseten cost caveat**: ran — `thinkingTokens: 0` in the open-weights file vs 3,043 on the Meta path; the "may be understated" footnote is accurate.
- **Viewer robustness**: read — unknown file/case in deep links falls back and rewrites the address ([main.ts:1016,789](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/viewer/src/main.ts)); boot failures surface in-page ([main.ts:1154](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/viewer/src/main.ts)); DOM built with `createElement`/`textContent`, `CSS.escape` on citations, `localStorage` in try/catch; writ export is a Blob download (no network); `check-viewer.ts` exercises compare/repair/why/scoreboard/phone/spotlight plus desktop pixel-invariance.
- **Harness error hygiene**: read — provider failures collapse to kind+HTTP status (no SDK body echo, [harness.ts:361-364](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/harness.ts)); `rawPreview` kept only on synthetic parse failures; repair never offered on declines; payer runs default out of the scoreboard.
- **Security/data**: ran — no secret patterns (`sk-`, private keys, `AKIA`) in results/synthetic; no `.env`; no SSN/phone/MRN/claim-ID patterns in the 50 cases; letters disclaim identifiers in code ([letters.ts:5,130](/tmp/claude-1000/-home-james-projects-your-procedure-is-denied-build/9fc98b9d-e5c7-45fe-9c8e-9ef9e757f00f/scratchpad/muse-review/build/src/synthetic/letters.ts)); only aliases/ages/sexes throughout.
- **Not verifiable here**: `npm test` / "263 tests" (no `node_modules`, registry unreachable), demo.hemeehr.com, Zenodo DOIs, the `litmus-gate` npm listing, and the "four corrected keys" narrative (history-dependent). None contradicted; all out of reach of this environment.

event.advisory_text: Exercise this the way the user will and judge it by the REAL result they'd get — the actual output a person experiences — not a proxy that can pass while it's broken (a syntax check, an HTTP 200, a DOM query, or a screenshot saved but never opened). When the real result is something only the eye can confirm — a rendered page, game, or UI — look at the render itself with a HEADLESS browser in the background (never a visible window that steals focus), not an inference from the DOM or logs. Scale the check to what this is — finish the WHOLE check in one pass, then stop once it's genuinely working rather than re-verifying — and fix and rerun anything that's off, without re-stating what was built until it's actually verified. Do that now with a tool.
